findings.b: Legacy rose from 26% to 28% of central government systems in a year, and the red-rated share rose too. Departments range widely, and some sit near 60%.

findings.t: COBOL still pays benefits and collects tax
findings.b: DWP's benefit systems were re-platformed in 2021 but remain COBOL. DWP was still hiring COBOL engineers in March 2026. HMRC still pays contractors to maintain COBOL.

findings.t: Skills risk was flagged in 2013 and is still live
findings.b: In 2013 the NAO warned that VME and COBOL skills would get harder to source at HMRC, and that DWP's COBOL knowledge was declining, among contractors too.

findings.t: Re-platforming buys time, it does not end the language
findings.b: Several big moves kept the old language on new hardware: DWP's VME-R and DVLA's managed mainframe. That reduces hardware risk while the COBOL skills risk remains.

findings.t: Fortran is old but not legacy in the same way
findings.b: The Met Office's next-generation model, LFRic, is still written in modern Fortran. Scientific Fortran is actively developed, so the risk there is HPC skills, not abandonment.

findings.t: Public code cannot see the legacy estate
findings.b: No COBOL repositories appear in 14 government GitHub organisations. Legacy code lives in private estates and supplier contracts, so audits and accounting officer assessments are the only window.
HMRC closed CHIEF after about 30 years, with no new declarations after July 2024. Police forces were migrated to LEDS in September 2025. Both took years longer than first planned.

languages.by: CODASYL committee, US Department of Defense initiative; drew on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC
languages.purpose: Business data processing: records, files, batch runs, money arithmetic.
languages.traits: English-like, verbose, fixed decimal arithmetic, strong batch and file handling. Fixed format echoes the 80-column card.
languages.gov: DWP benefits and pensions (Micro Focus COBOL); HMRC tax systems; formerly HMRC CHIEF and DWP VME systems.
languages.talent: Shrinking. Many experienced specialists are nearing retirement, and few new developers learn it. DWP still recruits for it.
languages.debt: Strong link. NAO named COBOL skills as a risk at HMRC and DWP in 2013.
languages.modern: Java, C# on .NET, or modern COBOL on Linux and cloud.
languages.repos: 0 repositories with COBOL as main language; 4 code mentions
languages.out: Long tail. Stable systems will keep running for a decade or more while skills get scarcer and dearer.

languages.by: IBM team led by John Backus
languages.traits: Fast array maths, strong compilers, modern versions (2003 onwards) add object orientation and parallelism.
languages.gov: Met Office Unified Model and its replacement LFRic; STFC, UKAEA and UKCEH research codes.
languages.talent: Niche but renewing through universities and HPC centres.
languages.debt: Weak link. The language is current; the old code style and HPC skills are the pressure points.
languages.modern: Modern Fortran with code generation (PSyclone); C++, Julia or Python for some tools.
languages.repos: 14 primary-language repositories in the 14-organisation scan; 28 across science organisations
languages.out: Stays. Weather and climate models will run on Fortran for years.

languages.purpose: Job control: telling an IBM mainframe which programs to run, in what order, with which files.
languages.traits: Terse card-image statements; batch schedules depend on it.
languages.gov: Likely wherever IBM Z mainframes run batch, such as the managed mainframe services used by DVLA and HMRC.
languages.talent: Tied to the mainframe pool; rarely taught.
languages.debt: Strong link through batch scheduling knowledge.
languages.modern: Workflow schedulers and cloud batch services.

languages.by: ICL (now Fujitsu); VME developed in the mid-1970s
languages.purpose: Mainframe operating system and its System Control Language.
languages.traits: Proprietary; ran UK revenue and benefit systems; vendor-specific COBOL dialect.
languages.gov: Formerly DWP's benefit systems and HMRC's CHIEF; HMRC VAT ran on VME in 2013.
languages.talent: Very small. Fujitsu stopped selling VME as a licensed product at the end of 2020.
languages.debt: Strong link. Government was called the world's biggest VME customer.
languages.modern: Open systems with modern COBOL, or rewrite.
languages.out: Ending. Fujitsu mainframe sales stop by 2030 and support by 2035.

languages.purpose: Programming language of SAP business systems.
languages.traits: Database-centred, report and transaction oriented; customisations live in ABAP.
languages.gov: HMRC's ETMP, which handles more than 40 taxes, is built on SAP. ABAP use inside ETMP is our inference.
languages.talent: Healthy commercial market, though S/4HANA migration demand is high across industry.
languages.debt: Medium. The base product's end of support forces the migration, not the language.
languages.modern: ABAP on S/4HANA (system conversion keeps customisations).

languages.purpose: 4GL and database for high-volume transaction systems.
languages.traits: Fast on mainframes; proprietary; small skills base.
languages.gov: A 2014 reader comment on DVLA's blog mentions Adabas databases. We have not confirmed current use.
languages.modern: Relational or cloud databases with Java or C#.

languages.purpose: Procedural code that runs inside Oracle databases.
languages.traits: Business rules held in stored procedures, close to the data.
languages.gov: Ministry of Justice prison data (NOMIS) tooling appears in public repositories.
languages.talent: Large but ageing database developer pool.
languages.debt: Medium. Logic locked in the database makes migration harder.
languages.modern: Application services plus PostgreSQL or managed databases.

languages.purpose: Text processing, scripting and early web applications.
languages.gov: Companies House's core web application repository lists Perl as its main language.
languages.debt: Medium. Older web estates depend on it.

languages.traits: Quick to build; tied to Windows and Office versions.
languages.gov: Widely reported in desktop tools across the public sector. Not measured in this scan.
languages.talent: Many casual users; few professional maintainers.
languages.debt: Hidden debt: end-user tools sit outside IT asset registers.
languages.out: Fades as Office automation moves to new tooling.

languages.traits: Portable, large ecosystem; old versions such as Java 8 now count as legacy in their own right.
languages.gov: Widely used for back-end services and as the main COBOL conversion target.

languages.purpose: Functional and object-oriented code on the JVM.
languages.traits: Expressive, strongly typed; HMRC's MDTP services are built in it.
languages.gov: HMRC's digital tax platform; 1,560 public repositories, most of them HMRC's.
languages.debt: Watch item: a niche skills pool could make this tomorrow's legacy.

languages.traits: Productive; GOV.UK publishing runs on it.
Runs in every browser; GOV.UK Frontend is written in it.
languages.debt: Low; dependency churn is the risk.

languages.gov: Home Office Design System and new services.

languages.traits: Common COBOL conversion target alongside Java.
languages.gov: .NET services and clients such as GOV.UK Notify's .NET client.
languages.debt: Low on current .NET; .NET Framework 4.x estates are a growing legacy.

languages.gov: HMRC tax calculator library; MoJ services.
MoJ Modernisation Platform, one of the main routes off legacy hosting.

systems.plat: Formerly ICL VME; now Micro Focus COBOL on open systems
systems.svc: State Pension, Jobseeker's Allowance, Income Support, Disability Living Allowance and other benefits
systems.plan: June 2025: DWP agreed a plan to modernise priority legacy benefit and pension services.

systems.sup: Aspire (Capgemini, Fujitsu) at the time of audit

systems.svc: Accounting for more than 40 taxes; about 40,000 daily users; over £800bn a year
systems.plan: Move to S/4HANA; decommission ECC6 in 2030.
No new declarations since July 2024; closure work due by March 2025. Replaced by the Customs Declaration Service.

systems.plat: Two mainframe-hosted systems with indexed master files
systems.plan: Merged into one cloud service; green-screen interface replaced.
Delivered over 18 months in two stages.

systems.svc: Arrests, convictions, wanted and missing people, vehicles and drivers for every UK force
systems.plan: Forces migrated to LEDS in September 2025; PNC to be switched off once dependence ends. Switch-off date not confirmed in our sources.

systems.svc: Records for over 53 million drivers and 47 million vehicles
systems.plan: Migrate all digital driver licensing services to the strategic cloud platform by March 2026.

systems.plat: Many platforms; 30% of applications unsupported in 2022
systems.svc: Trade, animal disease, flood and air quality services; 21 million transactions a year
systems.plan: Migrate 19 critical legacy applications to the cloud by March 2026.

systems.svc: National weather forecasts and climate projections
systems.sup: Met Office with STFC and universities
systems.plan: Replaced by LFRic, written in modern Fortran, for operational forecasting around 2027.
No legacy classification found. Shown because Perl is its main language.
Public repositories show PL/SQL services; legacy status not confirmed.

devolved_and_local.f: Replaces about 45 Health and Social Care patient record systems that cost about £6.5m a year to run. None had been switched off when audited; decommissioning is targeted for March 2029.
Contract expired in 2013 and was extended to 2030, 17 years, worth £42.4m. Its replacement is expected by October 2026, nearly five years late.
Contract expired in 2019 and was extended to July 2028. Phased replacement began in April 2025, due to finish by October 2027.
Contract extensions total 18 years, the longest in the portfolio. Its replacement, NIFAIS, was due in full operation by December 2025.
Legacy contracts were extended by almost eight years on average, a third of them by ten years or more. Reported skills gaps include software development and cyber security.
Replaces reliance on DWP's Central Payment System, which DWP is replacing. April 2025 to October 2027, about £33.2m.
Moves agriculture and rural economy services off legacy technologies and out of the Saughton House data centre. April 2024 to March 2027, about £14.6m.
Replaces inflexible legacy systems described as at high risk of failure. Due January 2027, about £9.35m.
Replaces most core operational systems. April 2024 to December 2028, about £15m.
Workforce capability assessment was slower than planned, so key digital skills gaps are not yet fully understood.
Supplier concentration in revenues and benefits, social care case management, electoral and planning systems. Leaving a revenues and benefits system could cost up to £300,000 per council.
About 18% of council IT posts were vacant in October 2023, and only 24% of councils had an ICT succession training programme.
The Spine Futures programme is rebuilding Spine services over two to three years, starting by moving the MESH messaging service to the cloud. Start year not stated in our source.

suppliers.r: VME platform owner; ran CHIEF under a £168.8m contract awarded without competition in 2020.
Long-running ETMP 'run and change' services at HMRC; rebuilt HMRC mainframe services on AWS and Azure.
Managed mainframe services for DVLA (zCloud). Reported to have also prepared HMRC's mainframe estate for cloud migration.
Awarded about £275m to migrate ETMP from ECC6 to S/4HANA.
Converted DWP's 11 VME benefit systems to Visual COBOL on open systems.

wider.b: Between 10% and 70% of police force technology estates count as legacy.
Between 10% and 50% of NHS trust estates count as legacy. The NHS security standard says no unsupported operating systems, software or browsers should be in use.
HM Courts and Tribunals Service finished moving out of old data centres in 2026 and is still retiring replaced applications.
The US GAO found that only 3 of 10 critical federal legacy systems flagged in 2019 had been modernised by 2025.

skills_evidence.b: Sourcing VME and COBOL skills would get harder. HMRC planned to recruit mainframe developers and set up succession plans and knowledge transfer.
COBOL skills and knowledge of the legacy system were declining, both in-house and among contractors.
Salary £44,447 to £59,813 to lead five engineers on Micro Focus COBOL systems that DWP calls central to its operational stability.
Half of organisations said their COBOL staff averaged 45 or older, and 46% already saw a shortage. The risk is fewer people entering the field, not the age of those in it.
About a quarter of COBOL professionals were 56 or older and 38% were 45 to 55. 63% of respondents named knowledge transfer as a top concern for future skills planning.
Enterprises lost 23% of specialist mainframe staff in five years; 63% of those posts stayed unfilled.

skills_and_debt.b: Departments keep systems running rather than change them, and pay a premium for contractors. HMRC still pays contractors top rates for COBOL work. COBOL systems also need extra software before they can share data through APIs.

Some systems with a shrinking skills base are very stable: the NAO called HMRC's VAT systems robust. And the 2012 survey found organisations could cross-train programmers in COBOL. The bigger drivers may be funding and supplier lock-in.
Re:State argues that legacy persists because capital comes as project money, not service money, and proposes a central taskforce with match funding.
Skills scarcity is a multiplier rather than the root cause. It raises the cost and risk of every change, which makes deferral look cheaper each year.

age_inclusive.b: 38% of civil servants were over 50 in 2022, up from 33% in 2010. Large delivery departments such as DWP, HMRC and MoD have older age profiles than policy departments.

48% of DWP staff were 50 or over, against 38% across the civil service. In 2023 DWP signed the Age-friendly Employer Pledge, covering age-positive hiring, flexible working and career development at all ages.
42% of councils cited retirement as a reason for IT staff turnover, and only 24% had a succession training programme for ICT staff.

Treat experienced specialists as teachers: recognise and pay for knowledge transfer, and offer phased retirement and flexible working. Open legacy roles to people of every age, including apprentices, career changers and returners. Age is a protected characteristic, so it must never stand in for skill in recruitment, selection or redundancy decisions.

routes.d: Move the system to new hosting, unchanged. Example: DVLA's managed mainframe service.
Move to a new platform with small changes, such as old COBOL to modern COBOL on Linux. Example: DWP's VME-R programme.
Replace with a product. HMRC's ETMP 'system conversion' keeps its customisations on the successor product.
Restructure or convert the code into a modern language, often with tools or AI.
Keep it, contain the risk, and wrap it with APIs. The NAO noted government once preferred these 'wrappers'.
Switch it off once a replacement carries the load. Example: HMRC's CHIEF after dual running with CDS.

steps.b: Register the system and score it with the Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework. A score of 16 or more makes it red-rated.
Map programs, batch jobs, data stores and interfaces. Extract the business rules, many of which are policy written into code. Remove dead code; one supplier reports up to 25% in large COBOL estates.
Write characterisation tests and capture real inputs and outputs, so the new system can be proved equivalent.
Pick from the 6 Rs per component, not per estate. Patterns such as strangler (replace piece by piece) reduce big-bang risk.
Translate, rewrite or reconfigure in slices, reviewing generated code with people who know the old system.
Move records and prove totals match. DWP moved about 11 billion database records in its conversion.
Run old and new side by side until the new one carries all load, as HMRC did with CHIEF and CDS.
Switch off, archive data lawfully, and end support contracts. Record the decommissioning on the legacy register.

ai_translation.b: Microsoft describes teams of AI agents that analyse COBOL, convert it to Java and generate tests. HCLTech reports large efficiency gains in a 2026 pilot.
IBM's software chief argues translation captures little of the real complexity. Rocket Software notes that code translation alone cannot reproduce decades of behaviour.
Infosys finds AI or tool conversion still needs COBOL subject experts to validate output, plus Java developers and mainframe knowledge.

AI shortens the reading and documenting stages most. It does not remove the need for equivalence tests, data reconciliation or people who understand the policy in the code. No UK government department has published results of AI conversion at scale.

decommissioning.e: No new declarations; closure work completed by March 2025
Police forces and agencies migrated to LEDS
All digital driver licensing services move to the strategic cloud platform (planned)
19 critical legacy applications migrated to the cloud (planned)
LFRic replaces it for operational forecasting (planned)
ECC6 decommissioned after move to S/4HANA (planned)

futures.b: Will run core benefits and tax for years. Expect fewer, dearer specialists, more re-platformed COBOL on cloud, and AI-assisted documentation before any wholesale rewrite.
VME ends with Fujitsu's mainframe exit in 2035. IBM Z continues, often bought as a managed service, so the question becomes contract and skills rather than hardware.
Remains the language of weather and climate. Risk moves to keeping HPC and code-generation skills.
Scala, Ruby and older Java and .NET versions are the next candidates for legacy. Workforce planning now is cheaper than remediation later.

learning_exists.t: Government Digital and Data Profession Capability Framework
learning_exists.b: Defines digital, data and technology roles and four skill levels: awareness, working, practitioner and expert.

learning_exists.t: Digital, data and AI skills commitment
learning_exists.b: GDS and departments provide learning pathways, apprenticeships and leadership development so every civil servant has enough digital understanding.
The share of civil servants working in digital and data rose from 2.8% in 2018 to 5% in 2023, with a stated aim of reducing reliance on contingent labour.
HMRC planned mainframe recruitment, succession plans and knowledge transfer in 2013. DWP built 'heritage reliability engineering' around its large legacy services.

learning_gaps.b: We found no public cross-government count of staff or contractors by programming language. Without it, skills risk cannot be set against the red-rated register.

learning_gaps.t: Legacy skills are not visible in the framework
learning_gaps.b: In this scan we did not find a role or skill in the capability framework for maintaining or migrating legacy languages. This needs confirming with the framework team.
Where suppliers run legacy systems, the system knowledge leaves with the contract. Reporting on HMRC records a watchdog call to grow its 'intelligent client' function.
Policy logic often exists only in code. Losing the people who know it is a service risk, not just an IT one.

learning_options.t: Add a legacy-language field to the legacy register
learning_options.b: Record language, platform, in-house and supplier headcount, and named knowledge holders for every red-rated system.
Pair legacy readers with modern engineers; teach COBOL and JCL reading, characterisation testing and data reconciliation.
Use AI-assisted documentation to turn code into reviewed, plain-English business rules held by the service owner.
Require suppliers to deliver documentation, tests and shadowing as contract outputs, not optional extras.
Track Scala, Ruby and end-of-support Java and .NET skills now, before they become scarce.

equality_impacts.t: People who rely on benefits and pensions
equality_impacts.b: DWP's COBOL systems pay State Pension and other benefits. When legacy systems fail or are slow to change, the effect falls hardest on people with the least financial cushion.
Defra handles around 14 million transactions a year that still involve paper forms. Paper can suit some people and exclude others, such as people with some visual impairments or those who move often.
Text-only mainframe screens often work poorly with assistive technology such as screen readers. We found no audit of this across government, so the scale is unknown.
Research cited by the LGA found 59% of the workforce cannot do all basic digital tasks. Upskilling plans need to start where people are, not where new systems assume they are.
Devolved and local bodies report legacy by contract, rarely by technology. Less visibility can mean less shared support, so people in some places may depend on older systems for longer.

Public bodies must have due regard to eliminating discrimination and advancing equality of opportunity. That applies to decommissioning plans, service changes and workforce decisions made during modernisation.

inclusive_routes.b: Government's digital skills commitment includes apprenticeships. Legacy reading and modernisation engineering could be built into them.
Government Science and Engineering publishes a returners pack. A similar route could bring back people who left technical roles, including former mainframe staff.
Survey evidence suggests programmers can be cross-trained in COBOL. Business knowledge is often the harder part to replace.
Pair each experienced specialist with a newer engineer on real changes, so knowledge moves through practice rather than documents alone.
Flexible working and phased retirement keep knowledge available for longer, on terms that suit the person.
Clear written specifications, predictable routines and quiet working suit many people, including many neurodivergent engineers, and suit legacy maintenance work well.

case_studies.t: DWP: moving 11 benefit systems off ICL VME
case_studies.ctx: Benefit systems from the 1980s ran on ICL VME mainframes in COBOL, with daytime online and overnight batch services.
case_studies.appr: Re-platformed one system at a time, starting with the smallest, converting COBOL to a modern dialect on open systems.
case_studies.out: All 11 systems moved by January 2021, about 25 million lines of code and 11 billion database records.
case_studies.less: Starting small built skills. Re-platforming removed the hardware risk but kept COBOL, so the skills risk remains.

case_studies.t: HMRC: retiring CHIEF for the Customs Declaration Service
case_studies.ctx: A customs system of about 30 years on VME, run through several outsourcing arrangements.
case_studies.appr: Built a new service and ran both in parallel, moving more than 6,000 declarants.
case_studies.out: No new declarations on CHIEF after July 2024; closure work due by March 2025.
case_studies.less: Dual running made retirement safe but took years longer than planned and needed contract extensions.

case_studies.t: Met Office: from the Unified Model to LFRic
case_studies.ctx: A 35-year-old Fortran model on a latitude-longitude grid that does not suit new supercomputers.
case_studies.appr: A new model in modern Fortran, with code generation (PSyclone) separating science from parallel code.
case_studies.less: Modernising does not always mean changing language; architecture and tooling can matter more.

case_studies.t: Home Office: replacing the Police National Computer
case_studies.ctx: A mainframe system from 1974 used by every UK police force.
case_studies.appr: After a 2021 reset, a focused programme to replace it with LEDS.
case_studies.out: Forces migrated to LEDS in September 2025; PNC to be switched off once dependence ends.
case_studies.less: Narrowing scope helped delivery; long overlap periods cost money to run both systems.

case_studies.ctx: The SAP platform behind more than 40 taxes and over £800bn a year faces end of mainstream support.
case_studies.appr: A system conversion to S/4HANA that keeps existing customisations, tested first in a sandbox.
case_studies.less: Forced by a product's end of support, not by the language; the choice of route still matters.

case_studies.t: Northern Ireland: encompass and the cost of overlap
case_studies.ctx: About 45 legacy patient record systems costing about £6.5m a year.
case_studies.appr: A single regional electronic record replacing them in stages.
case_studies.out: None of the legacy systems had been switched off when audited; target March 2029.
case_studies.less: Decommissioning needs its own plan and budget, or old systems run on alongside the new.

scenarios.t: Your key legacy specialist is leaving
steps: Agree a handover period and pay for knowledge transfer
Pair them with a newer engineer on live changes
Capture business rules in plain English, reviewed by the service owner
Record the risk against the system in the legacy register

scenarios.t: Your supplier contract ends within a year
steps: Ask for documentation, tests and code as contract deliverables
Compare a short extension with an exit plan
Price the exit, including data migration
Avoid repeated long extensions, a pattern audits criticise

scenarios.t: Your platform vendor announces end of support
steps: Check the published support dates
Decide between rehost on a supported platform and a route off the platform
Plan dual running before the cut-over
Set a decommissioning date and track it

scenarios.t: A supplier pitches AI code conversion
steps: Ask for evidence from comparable public sector work
Run a pilot on one module with equivalence tests written first
Keep legacy experts to validate the output
Measure behaviour, not lines converted

scenarios.t: An audit rates your system red
steps: Confirm the score with the Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework
Agree a remediation plan, as required for red-rated systems
Brief your board on service and skills risk
Set review dates

scenarios.t: You inherit a system nobody understands
steps: Map programs, jobs, data and interfaces
Remove dead code before anything else
Write characterisation tests from real inputs
Only then choose a route

themes.b: Unsupported systems cannot receive security fixes. The red-rated category includes systems with known vulnerabilities.
Long single-supplier arrangements and repeated extensions are a recurring pattern, from CHIEF to Northern Ireland's portfolio.
COBOL systems at HMRC need extra software to share data through APIs, which slows real-time data sharing.
MPs warned that legacy IT is a barrier to government's AI plans.
Capital is often allocated as project money rather than service money, which leaves maintenance underfunded.
Government aims to reduce reliance on contractors as its digital workforce grows.

personas.pains: Knowledge sits with a few people; the supplier contract renews next year.

personas.pains: No data on staff by programming language.

glossary.definition: Systems that are end-of-life, out of supplier support or impossible to update, as defined in government's review.
A legacy system scoring 16 or more on the Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework, the highest risk category.
The future cost of keeping a system running and changeable because of past shortcuts or ageing technology.
A large central computer built for high-volume, reliable transaction and batch processing.
Virtual Machine Environment, ICL's mainframe operating system, later owned by Fujitsu.
Common Business-Oriented Language, designed in 1959 for business data processing.
Formula Translation, IBM's 1957 language for numerical computing.
Job Control Language, which tells an IBM mainframe what to run and with which files.
IBM's transaction processing monitor for online mainframe applications.
A shared COBOL file describing a record layout, included by many programs.
Running large jobs in sequence, often overnight, rather than one transaction at a time.
A text-only terminal interface used with mainframes.
Updating or replacing legacy software so it is supported and can change at the pace services need.
Translating source code from one programming language to another.
Rehost, re-platform, repurchase, refactor, retain and retire: the common menu of migration routes.
Moving a system to new hosting without changing it.
Moving to a new platform with limited changes, such as new hardware or runtime.
Restructuring code, or converting it to a new language, without changing what it does.
Replacing a system piece by piece while the old one keeps running.
A software layer that lets old systems talk to new ones, often through APIs.
A test that records what existing code actually does, so a replacement can be proved equivalent.
Operating old and new systems in parallel during migration.
Switching off a system, archiving its data and closing its contracts.
An organisation's in-house capability to specify, manage and challenge suppliers.
Code that never runs and can be removed before migration.
Law Enforcement Data Service, the Police National Computer's replacement.
Enterprise Tax Management Platform, HMRC's SAP-based tax accounting system.
Customs Handling of Import and Export Freight, HMRC's retired customs system.
The Met Office's new modelling system, named after Lewis Fry Richardson.
